### 2000 census

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 2000 census")]

As of the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census")[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-GR2-23) of 2000, there were 19,440 people, 7,253 households, and 5,287 families living in the county. The [population density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_density "Population density") was 39 people per square mile (15 people/km 2). There were 7,981 housing units at an average density of 16 units per square mile (6.2 units/km 2). The racial makeup of the county was 56.89% [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)"), 41.26% [Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)") or [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)"), 0.19% [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)"), 0.17% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)"), 0.04% [Pacific Islander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)"), 0.99% from [other races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)"), and 0.46% from two or more races. 2.29% of the population were [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)") or [Latino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)") of any race.

According to the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census")[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-GR2-23) of 2000, the largest ancestry groups in Chickasaw County were [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_American "English American") 44.1%, [African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American "African American") 41% and [Scots-Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scots-Irish_American "Scots-Irish American") 13.5%.

There were 7,253 households, out of which 36.30% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 50.80% were [married couples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage "Marriage") living together, 18.00% had a female householder with no husband present, and 27.10% were non-families. 24.90% of all households were made up of individuals, and 11.90% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.65 and the average family size was 3.17.

In the county, the population was spread out, with 28.60% under the age of 18, 9.30% from 18 to 24, 27.60% from 25 to 44, 21.00% from 45 to 64, and 13.50% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 34 years. For every 100 females there were 92.60 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 87.40 males.

The median income for a household in the county was $26,364, and the median income for a family was $33,819. Males had a median income of $25,459 versus $20,099 for females. The [per capita income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_capita_income "Per capita income") for the county was $13,279. About 16.80% of families and 20.00% of the population were below the [poverty line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty_line "Poverty line"), including 23.90% of those under age 18 and 22.40% of those age 65 or over.

## Notable locals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Notable locals")]

*   Singer-songwriter [Bobbie Gentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobbie_Gentry "Bobbie Gentry"), a [Mississippi Musicians Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Musicians_Hall_of_Fame "Mississippi Musicians Hall of Fame") inductee
*   [Bukka White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukka_White "Bukka White"), early blues performer
*   [William Raspberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Raspberry "William Raspberry"), journalist
*   [Milan Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan_Williams "Milan Williams"), founding member of [The Commodores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Commodores "The Commodores")
*   [Jim Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Hood "Jim Hood"), politician and former Mississippi Attorney General
*   [Jeff Busby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Busby "Jeff Busby"), United States Representative who spearheaded the [Natchez Trace Parkway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natchez_Trace_Parkway "Natchez Trace Parkway")
*   [Shaquille Vance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaquille_Vance "Shaquille Vance"), 2012 U.S. Paralympic National Championship, gold medal (100m), silver medal (200m)
*   [Ida Mae Brandon Gladney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ida_Mae_Brandon_Gladney "Ida Mae Brandon Gladney"), central character in the Pulitzer Prize-winning nonfiction book _[The Warmth of Other Suns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Warmth\_of\_Other\_Suns "The Warmth of Other Suns")_ by [Isabel Wilkerson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabel_Wilkerson "Isabel Wilkerson")[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-26)

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

Candyland, the plantation of the fictional Calvin Candie, played by [Leonardo DiCaprio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_DiCaprio "Leonardo DiCaprio") in [Quentin Tarantino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quentin_Tarantino "Quentin Tarantino")'s film _[Django Unchained](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Django\_Unchained "Django Unchained")_, is located in Chickasaw County.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-27)

[Titus Andromedon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titus_Andromedon "Titus Andromedon"), from the Netflix series _[Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbreakable\_Kimmy\_Schmidt "Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt")_, is from Chickasaw County.

**Chickasaw County** is a [county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_(United_States) "County (United States)") located in the [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"). As of the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), the population was 17,106.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-1) Its [county seats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") are [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston,_Mississippi "Houston, Mississippi") and [Okolona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okolona,_Mississippi "Okolona, Mississippi").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-GR6-2) The county is named for the [Chickasaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw "Chickasaw") people, who lived in this area for hundreds of years. Most were [forcibly removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Removal "Indian Removal") to [Indian Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Territory "Indian Territory") in the 1830s, but some remained and became citizens of the state and the United States.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Mississippi state legislature created Chickasaw County in 1836, following the cession of the land by the [Chickasaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw "Chickasaw") Indians. It was quickly settled by Americans from the east, mainly from the Southern states. By the time of the Civil War, riverfront landings had been developed by the many large cotton plantations worked by [slaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slaves "Slaves"), who outnumbered the white residents of the county.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-Chickasaw_County_History-3)

The [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") devastated the local economy, completely destroying the plantation-based infrastructure of Chickasaw County. The newly freed slaves had to adapt to the new labor system, in which the white landowners still retained partial control over their lives through the practice of [sharecropping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharecropping "Sharecropping"). The economy declined again in the late 19th century, when falling cotton prices reduced both black and white residents to poverty. Farmers eventually began diversifying their crops, and the economy slowly began to improve.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-Chickasaw_County_History-3)

### 2020 census

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2020 census")]

As of the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), the county had a population of 17,106. The median age was 41.0 years. 22.7% of residents were under the age of 18 and 19.2% of residents were 65 years of age or older. For every 100 females there were 92.9 males, and for every 100 females age 18 and over there were 90.5 males age 18 and over.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-Census2020DP-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-Census2020PL-21)

The racial makeup of the county was 50.6% [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Americans "White Americans"), 43.5% [Black or African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans"), 0.2% [American Indian and Alaska Native](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States"), 0.3% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Americans "Asian Americans"), <0.1% [Native Hawaiian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Hawaiians "Native Hawaiians") and [Pacific Islander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Islander "Pacific Islander"), 2.5% from some other race, and 3.0% from [two or more races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiracial_Americans "Multiracial Americans"). [Hispanic or Latino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans "Hispanic and Latino Americans") residents of any race comprised 3.8% of the population.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-Census2020PL-21)

<0.1% of residents lived in urban areas, while 100.0% lived in rural areas.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-Census2020DHC-22)

There were 6,778 households in the county, of which 30.7% had children under the age of 18 living in them. Of all households, 40.3% were married-couple households, 18.7% were households with a male householder and no spouse or partner present, and 35.7% were households with a female householder and no spouse or partner present. About 29.6% of all households were made up of individuals and 12.9% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-Census2020DP-20)

There were 7,789 housing units, of which 13.0% were vacant. Among occupied housing units, 72.1% were owner-occupied and 27.9% were renter-occupied. The homeowner vacancy rate was 1.0% and the rental vacancy rate was 16.4%.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-Census2020DP-20)

### 2000 census

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 2000 census")]

As of the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census")[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-GR2-23) of 2000, there were 19,440 people, 7,253 households, and 5,287 families living in the county. The [population density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_density "Population density") was 39 people per square mile (15 people/km 2). There were 7,981 housing units at an average density of 16 units per square mile (6.2 units/km 2). The racial makeup of the county was 56.89% [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)"), 41.26% [Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)") or [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)"), 0.19% [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)"), 0.17% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)"), 0.04% [Pacific Islander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)"), 0.99% from [other races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)"), and 0.46% from two or more races. 2.29% of the population were [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)") or [Latino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)") of any race.

According to the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census")[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi#cite_note-GR2-23) of 2000, the largest ancestry groups in Chickasaw County were [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_American "English American") 44.1%, [African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American "African American") 41% and [Scots-Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scots-Irish_American "Scots-Irish American") 13.5%.

There were 7,253 households, out of which 36.30% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 50.80% were [married couples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage "Marriage") living together, 18.00% had a female householder with no husband present, and 27.10% were non-families. 24.90% of all households were made up of individuals, and 11.90% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.65 and the average family size was 3.17.

In the county, the population was spread out, with 28.60% under the age of 18, 9.30% from 18 to 24, 27.60% from 25 to 44, 21.00% from 45 to 64, and 13.50% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 34 years. For every 100 females there were 92.60 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 87.40 males.

The median income for a household in the county was $26,364, and the median income for a family was $33,819. Males had a median income of $25,459 versus $20,099 for females. The [per capita income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_capita_income "Per capita income") for the county was $13,279. About 16.80% of families and 20.00% of the population were below the [poverty line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty_line "Poverty line"), including 23.90% of those under age 18 and 22.40% of those age 65 or over.

Chickasaw County

# Chickasaw County

 4 minutes to read

Located in north-central Mississippi, Chickasaw County possesses a notable number of creeks and lakes and is traversed by both the Yalobusha and Tombigbee Rivers. Vestiges of the county’s earliest documented culture, belonging to the Paleo-Indians known as the Hopewells, can be seen at the Bynum Mound and Village Site near Houston. The French and British also occupied Chickasaw lands during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Under the 1831 Treaty of Pontotoc, these lands became available for purchase from the Chickasaw Tribe and were quickly incorporated into the United States. The county takes its name from the region’s native inhabitants and was formally established on 9 February 1836. Chickasaw’s two county seats are Okolona and Houston, the latter named for the distinguished leader of the Texas war of independence, Gen. Sam Houston.

In 1840 Chickasaw was home to 2,148 free whites, 1 free African American, and 806 slaves. Early on, the county was almost entirely agricultural, and the plantation economy was central to Chickasaw’s antebellum prosperity. By 1860 the county had changed substantially. Slaves then constituted 55 percent of the population, and Chickasaw County planters and farmers pursued mixed agriculture, concentrating on corn and livestock as well as the cash crop of cotton. Following the construction of the Mobile and Ohio Railroad through Chickasaw in 1859, the county’s main sphere of commercial activity shifted from Houston to Okolona. While only eighty-three residents of Chickasaw County were employed in industry in 1860, its manufacturing sector produced a substantial variety of commodities, including fixed agricultural implements, flour and meal, lumber, boots, carriages, furniture, and saddles and harnesses.

As in much of Mississippi, most of Chickasaw’s antebellum congregants attended Baptist or Methodist churches. Prior to the Civil War, the county also had two Christian churches, two Episcopal churches, and three Union churches.

Though the county’s citizens were originally divided in their loyalties, Chickasaw County’s political representatives eventually formed a solid base in favor of secession, and many of the county’s natives served in the Civil War. In addition to several attempts by federal troops to destroy the stretch of the Mobile and Ohio Railroad running through the county, a number of battles and raids took place in Chickasaw. Property owners in the county suffered losses on many fronts as a result of the war, especially in the destruction of the county’s economic infrastructure.

Chickasaw was considered among the state’s postbellum “black districts,” as following the war its political boundaries were redrawn to ensure the election of African American candidates. Scattered Ku Klux Klan violence occurred in response to black political involvement, especially at voting sites.

The county’s population struggled during the postbellum era. In 1872 Clay and Webster Counties annexed portions of Chickasaw. Though agriculture remained the county’s primary subsistence activity, the demise of Chickasaw’s plantation economy led to the rise of small farms and sharecropping. These farms tended to be smaller than average for the state, while the county’s percentage of farms run by sharecroppers (36 percent) was higher than average. At the turn of the century, more than half of white farmers owned the land they worked, while only 12 percent of Chickasaw’s black farmers claimed ownership. The county’s industrial workforce also remained relatively small, with manufacturing firms employing just seventy-eight people.

Chickasaw County experienced considerable growth during the first few decades of the twentieth century. By 1900 the county’s population had grown to almost twenty thousand, and in 1909 the county constructed Mississippi’s first Carnegie Library in Houston. Chickasaw also saw a rise in industrial activity during this era, and its agricultural economy moved away from cotton cultivation toward livestock.

By 1916 more than half of the Chickasaw’s church members were Baptists—mostly either Missionary Baptists or Southern Baptists. Smaller but still significant numbers of congregants attended the Methodist Episcopal Church, the Colored Methodist Episcopal Church, and the Presbyterian Church. Chickasaw County was home to notable religious musicians, including shape-note singer W. A. Beasley and the Pilgrim Jubilees gospel group.

Frank Burkitt, a Populist editor and political figure, was a Chickasaw County native, as was Pauline Orr, an important figure at the Mississippi University for Women. Blues musician Booker “Bukka” White was born in Houston in 1909. Country singer Bobbie Gentry, known for her rendition of “Ode to Billie Joe,” was likewise born in Chickasaw and mentioned the county often in her music. Chickasaw has long been home to Sparta Opry, a live country music show. William Raspberry, a Pulitzer Prize–winning journalist, grew up in Okolona and graduated from Okolona College High School in 1952.

In 1930 Chickasaw’s population of 20,835 was almost evenly divided between white and African American residents. Only about 29 percent of farmers owned their own land. Twenty years later, only 220 people were still involved in agriculture, while more than half of the workforce, almost 5,000 people, held manufacturing positions, largely in timber and textiles.

# Chickasaw County

 4 minutes to read

Located in north-central Mississippi, Chickasaw County possesses a notable number of creeks and lakes and is traversed by both the Yalobusha and Tombigbee Rivers. Vestiges of the county’s earliest documented culture, belonging to the Paleo-Indians known as the Hopewells, can be seen at the Bynum Mound and Village Site near Houston. The French and British also occupied Chickasaw lands during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Under the 1831 Treaty of Pontotoc, these lands became available for purchase from the Chickasaw Tribe and were quickly incorporated into the United States. The county takes its name from the region’s native inhabitants and was formally established on 9 February 1836. Chickasaw’s two county seats are Okolona and Houston, the latter named for the distinguished leader of the Texas war of independence, Gen. Sam Houston.

In 1840 Chickasaw was home to 2,148 free whites, 1 free African American, and 806 slaves. Early on, the county was almost entirely agricultural, and the plantation economy was central to Chickasaw’s antebellum prosperity. By 1860 the county had changed substantially. Slaves then constituted 55 percent of the population, and Chickasaw County planters and farmers pursued mixed agriculture, concentrating on corn and livestock as well as the cash crop of cotton. Following the construction of the Mobile and Ohio Railroad through Chickasaw in 1859, the county’s main sphere of commercial activity shifted from Houston to Okolona. While only eighty-three residents of Chickasaw County were employed in industry in 1860, its manufacturing sector produced a substantial variety of commodities, including fixed agricultural implements, flour and meal, lumber, boots, carriages, furniture, and saddles and harnesses.

As in much of Mississippi, most of Chickasaw’s antebellum congregants attended Baptist or Methodist churches. Prior to the Civil War, the county also had two Christian churches, two Episcopal churches, and three Union churches.

Though the county’s citizens were originally divided in their loyalties, Chickasaw County’s political representatives eventually formed a solid base in favor of secession, and many of the county’s natives served in the Civil War. In addition to several attempts by federal troops to destroy the stretch of the Mobile and Ohio Railroad running through the county, a number of battles and raids took place in Chickasaw. Property owners in the county suffered losses on many fronts as a result of the war, especially in the destruction of the county’s economic infrastructure.

Chickasaw was considered among the state’s postbellum “black districts,” as following the war its political boundaries were redrawn to ensure the election of African American candidates. Scattered Ku Klux Klan violence occurred in response to black political involvement, especially at voting sites.

The county’s population struggled during the postbellum era. In 1872 Clay and Webster Counties annexed portions of Chickasaw. Though agriculture remained the county’s primary subsistence activity, the demise of Chickasaw’s plantation economy led to the rise of small farms and sharecropping. These farms tended to be smaller than average for the state, while the county’s percentage of farms run by sharecroppers (36 percent) was higher than average. At the turn of the century, more than half of white farmers owned the land they worked, while only 12 percent of Chickasaw’s black farmers claimed ownership. The county’s industrial workforce also remained relatively small, with manufacturing firms employing just seventy-eight people.

Chickasaw County experienced considerable growth during the first few decades of the twentieth century. By 1900 the county’s population had grown to almost twenty thousand, and in 1909 the county constructed Mississippi’s first Carnegie Library in Houston. Chickasaw also saw a rise in industrial activity during this era, and its agricultural economy moved away from cotton cultivation toward livestock.

By 1916 more than half of the Chickasaw’s church members were Baptists—mostly either Missionary Baptists or Southern Baptists. Smaller but still significant numbers of congregants attended the Methodist Episcopal Church, the Colored Methodist Episcopal Church, and the Presbyterian Church. Chickasaw County was home to notable religious musicians, including shape-note singer W. A. Beasley and the Pilgrim Jubilees gospel group.

Frank Burkitt, a Populist editor and political figure, was a Chickasaw County native, as was Pauline Orr, an important figure at the Mississippi University for Women. Blues musician Booker “Bukka” White was born in Houston in 1909. Country singer Bobbie Gentry, known for her rendition of “Ode to Billie Joe,” was likewise born in Chickasaw and mentioned the county often in her music. Chickasaw has long been home to Sparta Opry, a live country music show. William Raspberry, a Pulitzer Prize–winning journalist, grew up in Okolona and graduated from Okolona College High School in 1952.

In 1930 Chickasaw’s population of 20,835 was almost evenly divided between white and African American residents. Only about 29 percent of farmers owned their own land. Dairy farming and cattle became increasingly central to Chickasaw’s agricultural sector during the first half of the twentieth century, while sweet potato cultivation increased following World War II. The county’s industrial force was also growing, employing 224 workers in 1930. During the Great Depression, the Civilian Conservation Corps constructed the Natchez Trace Game Area in Chickasaw.

By 1960 Chickasaw County’s population had dropped below 17,000, and almost two-thirds of residents were white. Twenty years later, only 220 people were still involved in agriculture, while more than half of the workforce, almost 5,000 people, held manufacturing positions, largely in timber and textiles.

Like many central Mississippi counties, in 2010 Chickasaw County’s population of 17,932 was predominantly white and had not changed significantly in size since 1960. However, a small but significant Latino/Hispanic minority had emerged.

Chickasaw County is a county located in the U.S. state of Mississippi. As of the 2020 census, the population was 17,106. Its county seats are Houston and Okolona. Land and property records can place an ancestor in a particular location, provide economic information, and reveal family relationships. Land records include: deeds, abstracts and indexes, mortgages, leases, grants and land patents.

See [Mississippi Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Land_and_Property "Mississippi Land and Property") for additional information about early Mississippi land ownership. After land was transferred to private ownership, subsequent transactions were usually recorded at the county courthouse and where records are currently housed.

Probate records are held by the Chickasaw County, Mississippi Genealogy Clerk of Court and are housed at the Chickasaw County, Mississippi Genealogy Courthouse. Microfilmed records can be found online at [Mississippi Probate Records, 1781-1930](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2036959). See the wiki page [Mississippi Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Probate_Records "Mississippi Probate Records") for information about how to use probate records.

_**Content:**_ Probate Records may give the decedent's date of death, names of his or her spouse, children, parents, siblings, in-laws, neighbors, associates, relatives, and their place of residence.

_**Record types:**_ Wills, estates, guardianships, naturalizations, and adoptions.

### Vital Records[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi_Genealogy&veaction=edit&section=37 "Edit section: Vital Records") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi_Genealogy&action=edit&section=37 "Edit section: Vital Records")]

[Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Vital_Records "United States Vital Records") consist of [births](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Birth_Records "United States Birth Records"), adoptions, [marriages](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Marriage_Records "United States Marriage Records"), divorces, and [deaths](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Death_Records "United States Death Records") recorded on registers, certificates, and documents. Mississippi law did not require keeping birth or death records until 1912. Births and deaths are kept by the Mississippi Bureau of Vital Statistics. Marriage records are kept by the county. See also [How to order Mississippi Vital Records](http://www.genealogyinc.com/mississippi) or [order electronically online](http://www.genealogyinc.com/ordervitalcertificate/).

See [Mississippi Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Vital_Records "Mississippi Vital Records") for more information on getting Mississippi records.

_**Civil War Battle**_  
 The following Civil War Battle was fought in Chickasaw County:[[8]](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Chickasaw_County,_Mississippi_Genealogy#cite_note-8)

Probate records are held by the Chickasaw County, Mississippi Genealogy Clerk of Court and are housed at the Chickasaw County, Mississippi Genealogy Courthouse. Microfilmed records can be found online at [Mississippi Probate Records, 1781-1930](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2036959). See the wiki page [Mississippi Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Probate_Records "Mississippi Probate Records") for information about how to use probate records.

_**Content:**_ Probate Records may give the decedent's date of death, names of his or her spouse, children, parents, siblings, in-laws, neighbors, associates, relatives, and their place of residence.

_**Record types:**_ Wills, estates, guardianships, naturalizations, and adoptions.

[Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Vital_Records "United States Vital Records") consist of [births](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Birth_Records "United States Birth Records"), adoptions, [marriages](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Marriage_Records "United States Marriage Records"), divorces, and [deaths](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Death_Records "United States Death Records") recorded on registers, certificates, and documents. Mississippi law did not require keeping birth or death records until 1912. Births and deaths are kept by the Mississippi Bureau of Vital Statistics. Marriage records are kept by the county. See also [How to order Mississippi Vital Records](http://www.genealogyinc.com/mississippi) or [order electronically online](http://www.genealogyinc.com/ordervitalcertificate/).
